name: Acorn Woodpecker
description: The Acorn Woodpecker is a social woodpecker of oak and pine-oak woodland, recognized by its red crown and strongly contrasting face. Family groups collect acorns and store them in holes made in trees or other wooden surfaces, guarding these food supplies together. They also catch insects and use tree cavities for nesting. Cooperative breeding and shared food storage make their behavior especially interesting, while their calls and movements often reveal an active group before every bird is visible.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Allen's Hummingbird
description: Allen's Hummingbird is a small coastal hummingbird with coppery sides, a green back, and a brilliant orange-red throat in adult males. It breeds along the Pacific Coast, using scrub, chaparral, and nearby woodland. Nectar supplies much of its energy, while small insects provide additional nutrients. Males perform elaborate courtship flights with steep dives and sounds produced by their tail feathers. Some populations migrate to Mexico, while others remain in southern California throughout the year.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: American Avocet
description: The American Avocet is a long-legged shorebird recognized by its slender, upturned bill and contrasting black-and-white wings. It feeds in shallow wetlands, sweeping its partly open bill through the water to capture small aquatic animals. Salt ponds, marshes, and mudflats provide important feeding habitat. Avocets often gather with other shorebirds and nest on sparsely vegetated ground near water, where their shallow nest scrapes can be difficult to distinguish from the surrounding surface.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: American Coot
description: The American Coot is a dark waterbird with a contrasting white bill, often seen swimming among ducks on lakes and ponds. Despite that resemblance, it belongs to the rail family. Lobed toes help it move through water and across soft ground. It eats mainly aquatic vegetation, taking additional foods when available, and may graze on land. Large winter flocks can gather on open water, while breeding birds use wetland vegetation for nesting and cover.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: American Dipper
description: The American Dipper is a compact gray songbird adapted to fast-flowing streams in western North and Central America. It searches for aquatic insects by wading, swimming, and diving, often disappearing beneath moving water that would challenge many other songbirds. Frequent bobbing movements give the bird its name. Rocks and fallen wood provide resting places between feeding trips. Its close association with streams makes water quality and suitable streambed habitat important parts of its environment.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: American Goldfinch
description: The American Goldfinch is a seed-eating songbird whose appearance changes markedly with the seasons. Breeding males wear bright yellow plumage with black wings and a black cap; females and winter birds are more subdued. These agile finches feed on seedheads and readily visit gardens and feeders. They nest relatively late in summer, when plants such as thistles provide both nesting material and abundant food. Their gently undulating flight often reveals white markings on the dark wings.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: American Robin
description: The American Robin is a widespread North American thrush with a warm orange breast and a familiar, musical song. Although often seen on lawns searching for earthworms, it also inhabits forests, parks, and mountain landscapes. Its diet includes insects and fruit, with berries becoming especially important outside the breeding season. Robins build cup-shaped nests and may gather in large communal roosts. Watching one pause between short runs often reveals its careful search for food on the ground.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: American White Pelican
description: The American White Pelican is an immense waterbird with broad white wings, contrasting dark flight feathers, and a large pouched bill. It catches fish from the water's surface, sometimes feeding cooperatively with other pelicans to concentrate prey in the shallows. Unlike the Brown Pelican, it does not normally plunge-dive from the air. Breeding colonies occupy relatively isolated sites near inland waters, while migration and winter bring many birds to coastal wetlands and sheltered bays.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Anna's Hummingbird
description: Anna's Hummingbird is a familiar resident of western gardens, coastal scrub, and open woodland. Adult males can flash an iridescent rose-pink head and throat, although the same feathers may appear dark when the light changes. The birds feed on nectar and small insects, moving between flowers with precise hovering flights. Males also perform dramatic aerial courtship displays. Unlike many hummingbirds that make long seasonal migrations, Anna's often remains in suitable parts of its range throughout the year.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Barn Owl
description: Barn owls are pale, long-winged predators associated with open fields, grassland, and quiet roosting places. Their heart-shaped facial disk helps direct sound toward their ears as they search for small mammals in darkness. In North America, the species is now commonly called the American Barn Owl. It often nests in buildings or cavities and gives rasping calls rather than the familiar hoots of many other owls. Young birds remain dependent on their parents while developing their hunting skills.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Belted Kingfisher
description: The Belted Kingfisher is a stocky, large-headed bird with a shaggy crest and a strong, straight bill. It watches rivers, lakes, and sheltered shorelines from exposed perches, then dives to catch fish and other aquatic prey. A loud rattling call often announces its arrival. Blue-gray upperparts contrast with a white collar and breast; females also have a rusty band below. Nesting pairs excavate burrows in earthen banks, linking their breeding habitat to both suitable soil and productive nearby water.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Bewick's Wren
description: Bewick's Wren is a lively brown-and-gray songbird with a bold pale eyebrow and a long tail that it frequently holds upright. It moves through shrubs, brush piles, and woodland edges, searching vegetation for insects and other small invertebrates. Despite its small size, its varied songs can carry well beyond the thicket where it is hidden. Dense native shrubs provide both feeding opportunities and shelter, while cavities offer places to nest.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Black Phoebe
description: The Black Phoebe is a small flycatcher with dark upperparts, a contrasting white belly, and a habit of repeatedly dipping its tail. It watches from low, exposed perches before flying out to catch insects. Streams, ponds, gardens, and coastal edges can all provide suitable hunting grounds. Access to water also supplies mud for its cup-shaped nest, which it attaches beneath sheltered structures such as bridges, overhangs, and building ledges.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Black Skimmer
description: The Black Skimmer is a long-winged coastal bird with contrasting dark upperparts and pale underparts. Its unusual bill has a lower half longer than the upper, allowing it to skim the water's surface in flight and detect small fish by touch. Beaches, sandbars, and protected shorelines provide resting and nesting sites. Groups often gather closely on open ground between feeding trips. Their specialized feeding technique and striking silhouettes make them distinctive among the gulls and terns that share their habitat.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Black-necked Stilt
description: The Black-necked Stilt combines sharply contrasting black-and-white plumage with exceptionally long pink legs and a straight, slender bill. It walks through shallow wetlands, mudflats, and salt ponds, picking small aquatic animals from the water or surface below. Stilts often occur alongside avocets and other shorebirds. During breeding, they place simple nests near water and actively defend the surrounding area, making their calls and alert postures conspicuous features of a wetland colony.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Black-tailed Deer
description: Black-tailed deer are coastal forms of mule deer associated with western North American forests, woodland edges, and meadows. Their dark tails and large ears are useful features, although appearance varies with age and season. They feed on grasses, leaves, and other vegetation, often moving between sheltered cover and more open feeding areas. This album keeps the broad Black-tailed Deer label rather than assigning a particular subspecies without additional identification information.

references.title: National Park Service

name: Black-tailed Jackrabbit
description: Despite its name, the Black-tailed Jackrabbit is a hare, distinguished by long hind legs, very large ears, and a dark stripe along the upper surface of its tail. It inhabits open country across much of the western United States and parts of Mexico. Grasses and other vegetation form its diet. Its ears help release body heat as well as detect danger, while powerful running and bounding provide an escape from predators.

references.title: National Park Service

name: Blister Beetle
description: Blister beetles belong to the family Meloidae, a varied group with elongated bodies and relatively soft wing covers. Adults often feed on plants and can gather around flowers, where some eat pollen and nectar. Their name comes from cantharidin, a defensive chemical that can blister skin. Many have a broad head and a noticeably narrower section behind it. This album retains the broader family identification, allowing the photograph's body shape, markings, and textures to be appreciated without assigning an uncertain species name.

references.title: University of Kentucky Department of Entomology: Blister Beetles

name: Botta's Pocket Gopher
description: Botta's Pocket Gopher is a burrowing rodent that spends much of its life in underground tunnels. It feeds on roots, tubers, and other plant material, sometimes bringing vegetation below ground. External cheek pouches help transport food, while strong forelimbs and prominent incisors assist with excavation. Fresh soil mounds often reveal its presence before the animal itself becomes visible. An appearance at a burrow entrance offers a brief view of an otherwise largely hidden mammal.

references.title: National Park Service

name: Brandt's Cormorant
description: Brandt's Cormorant is a large diving seabird closely associated with the Pacific Coast of North America. It searches underwater for fish and other marine prey, often using productive nearshore waters and kelp beds. Breeding adults develop vivid blue throat skin and fine pale feathers around the head and neck. Rocky islands and coastal cliffs provide places to rest and breed. Groups gathered on offshore rocks offer a view of the species' social behavior between repeated fishing dives.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Brewer's Blackbird
description: Brewer's Blackbird is a social, ground-feeding bird of open landscapes and towns in western North America. In sunlight, males show blue and green iridescence across otherwise black feathers, together with a striking pale eye. Females are mostly brown and less glossy. These adaptable birds search lawns, fields, and sidewalks for insects, seeds, and other food, then gather on wires or in trees. Changing light can make the male's plumage look surprisingly different between photographs.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Bushtit
description: The Bushtit is a tiny, long-tailed songbird usually encountered as part of a busy flock. Groups move through shrubs and woodland edges, keeping in touch with soft calls while inspecting leaves and twigs for insects and spiders. Individuals often hang upside down to reach food beneath foliage. Their nests are equally distinctive: elongated, hanging pouches woven from plant material and spider silk. The flock's constant movement often makes a clear view brief but rewarding.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: California Brown Pelican
description: The Brown Pelican is a large coastal seabird with a long bill and an expandable throat pouch. Along the Pacific Coast, it often travels in lines just above the waves or rests on offshore rocks, beaches, and harbor structures. It catches fish by diving from the air, then drains water from its pouch before swallowing its prey. Brown Pelicans nest in colonies, and their slow-looking wingbeats contrast with the speed and force of a fishing dive.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: California Condor
description: The California Condor is an immense scavenging bird whose broad wings allow it to travel long distances on rising air. Adults have mostly black plumage, pale patches beneath the wings, and a largely bare head. Condors feed on animal carcasses and often nest in sheltered cliff cavities. Captive breeding and reintroduction have been central to their recovery after severe historical declines. Their long-term survival still depends on conservation work, including reducing exposure to lead in scavenged food. Wing tags link photographs to individual histories: Haku (#77) is a female hatched in 1992, Little Stinker (#726) is a female hatched in 2014, and Chull (#1180) is a male hatched in 2022. Named captions use readable tags or a matching adjacent photo in the same sequence. Other photographs retain broader labels where the tag cannot be read confidently.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds
Friends of California Condors Wild and Free: Haku (#77)
Ventana Wildlife Society: Little Stinker (#726)
Ventana Wildlife Society: Chull (#1180)
Condor Spotter: individual records, hatch dates, and wing tags
National Park Service: identifying condors at Pinnacles

name: California Ground Squirrel
description: The California Ground Squirrel is a mottled gray-brown squirrel that uses burrows for shelter and protection. It occupies a variety of open habitats and woodland edges, often feeding close enough to retreat underground quickly. Seeds, nuts, fruits, and other available foods form its varied diet. Its bushy tail and upright alert posture can be conspicuous, but much of its daily activity takes place low to the ground as it moves between feeding spots and burrow entrances.

references.title: National Park Service

name: California Gull
description: The California Gull links inland western wetlands with the Pacific Coast. It often breeds in colonies on lake islands or levees, then moves toward coastal areas outside the breeding season. An opportunistic feeder, it takes insects, fish, and many other available foods. Young birds have mottled brown plumage that changes as they mature, making age important in identification. Adults are medium-sized gulls with gray backs, white heads, and yellowish legs.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: California Mountain Kingsnake
description: The California Mountain Kingsnake is a secretive, nonvenomous snake patterned with alternating red, black, and pale bands. It occupies suitable woodland, chaparral, and mountain habitats, spending much of its time hidden beneath cover or in crevices. Its diet includes lizards, other snakes, and small mammals. Although its colors can make it conspicuous when exposed, opportunities to see it are often brief. Rock formations and other natural cover are important parts of its habitat.

references.title: California Herps

name: California Quail
description: The California Quail is a ground-dwelling bird of scrub, chaparral, foothills, and nearby gardens. Its forward-curving head plume gives it an immediately recognizable silhouette. Groups called coveys move between feeding areas and protective cover, searching the ground for seeds, leaves, and small invertebrates. Nests are usually concealed at ground level. Watching a covey reveals a mixture of careful pauses, quick runs, and frequent calls as the birds maintain contact with one another.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: California Sea Lion
description: The California Sea Lion is a social marine mammal with visible ear flaps, broad front flippers, and a long snout. Adult males are substantially larger and usually darker than females. It feeds mainly on fish and squid in coastal waters, then returns to rocks, beaches, or structures such as buoys to rest. Barking calls and close groupings make resting colonies conspicuous. Its body shape and external ears help distinguish it from the harbor seals that may use nearby waters.

references.title: NOAA Fisheries

name: California Tarantula
description: This album uses the broad California Tarantula label because the exact species has not been established. Tarantulas are large, hairy spiders with eight legs, belonging to the arachnids rather than the insects. Many spend long periods in sheltered burrows and hunt insects or other small animals, often becoming more active in cooler conditions. Body color alone can be misleading for identification, so a precise species name is left open rather than inferred from this photograph.

references.title: National Park Service: tarantula natural history

name: California Towhee
description: The California Towhee is a sturdy, mostly brown sparrow associated with chaparral, brushy woodland edges, and gardens along the Pacific side of North America. Its plain appearance is offset by a warm patch beneath the tail and a sharp, metallic call. It commonly searches on the ground for seeds and other food, staying close to cover. Pairs are conspicuous around familiar territories, and individuals sometimes challenge their reflections in windows or car mirrors.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Canada Goose
description: The Canada Goose is a large waterbird with a black head and neck, a pale cheek patch, and a brown body. It uses lakes, marshes, fields, and many urban green spaces, feeding mainly on plants. Pairs often remain together across breeding seasons, and family groups can be conspicuous near water. Migrating flocks are known for their calls and coordinated formations, although some populations stay in suitable areas throughout the year. Young birds change rapidly from downy goslings to feathered juveniles.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Caspian Tern
description: The Caspian Tern is the world's largest tern, with a substantial red bill, pale body, and dark crown. It uses both coastal and inland waters, searching for fish from the air before diving toward the surface. Its strong proportions and deep, raspy calls help separate it from smaller terns. Breeding colonies occupy open ground near productive feeding waters. A bird passing overhead provides a clear view of the broad wings and heavy bill that characterize this powerful seabird.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Cattle Egret
description: Cattle egrets are compact white herons that often feed in grassy fields rather than standing in open water. They take insects and other small prey disturbed by grazing animals or machinery, making pastureland a productive hunting place. Breeding birds develop warmer coloring on parts of the head and body. The Western Cattle-Egret has spread well beyond its original African range, including to the Americas and Hawaii. The broader Cattle Egret label is retained for this album.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Chipmunk
description: This album keeps a broad chipmunk label while the exact identification remains open. Chipmunks are small members of the squirrel family that gather seeds, nuts, and other foods, often carrying them in expandable cheek pouches. Stripes on the face and body are useful identification clues, especially when comparing chipmunks with similar ground squirrels. Habitat, locality, and additional views can help distinguish species; the photograph is not assigned a more specific name without that supporting information.

references.title: National Park Service: chipmunk comparison

name: Chipping Sparrow
description: The Chipping Sparrow is a small, slender sparrow of open woodland, parks, and gardens with scattered trees. Breeding adults have a rusty crown, pale face, and dark eye-line, while winter plumage is softer and browner. It feeds mainly on seeds outside the breeding season and adds more insects while raising young. Much feeding takes place on the ground, with nearby shrubs offering cover. Careful attention to its head pattern helps distinguish it from other small brown sparrows.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Cinnamon Teal
description: The Cinnamon Teal is a small dabbling duck of shallow wetlands. Breeding males have rich reddish-brown plumage and red eyes, while females and nonbreeding birds are mottled brown and can resemble other teal. Its relatively long, broad bill helps with feeding near the surface and among aquatic vegetation. Marshes, flooded fields, and slow-moving waters provide habitat. Seasonal plumage changes make it useful to compare photographs from different times of year rather than relying on color alone.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Common Gallinule
description: The Common Gallinule is a marsh bird that moves between open water and dense vegetation. Adults have dark plumage, a red forehead shield and bill, and a white stripe along each side. Long toes help it walk across floating plants and soft mud, while it swims readily despite lacking webbed feet. Listen for clucks and whinnying calls from the reeds. Its combination of swimming, climbing, and walking makes wetland edges especially rewarding places to watch its behavior.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Common Merganser
description: The Common Merganser is a streamlined diving duck with a narrow, toothed bill suited to catching fish. Adult males have dark green heads and largely white bodies; females have gray bodies and reddish-brown, crested heads. Rivers and clear lakes provide feeding habitat, and suitable tree cavities offer nesting places. Outside the breeding season, birds may gather on larger bodies of water. A bird resting on a midstream rock can offer a clear view between repeated fishing dives.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Common Myna
description: The Common Myna is an adaptable starling relative with a brown body, dark head, bright facial skin, and conspicuous pale wing patches in flight. Native to Asia, it has been introduced in many other regions, including Hawaii. It searches lawns, fields, and developed areas for insects, fruit, and a wide range of other food. Social groups gather at communal roosts, where their varied calls can make them much easier to locate than quieter birds sharing the same trees.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Common Raven
description: The Common Raven is a large, adaptable member of the crow family found across much of the Northern Hemisphere. Its heavy bill, shaggy throat, deep calls, and broad wings give it a distinctive presence. Ravens occupy habitats ranging from deserts and mountains to forests and coastal areas. They eat a wide variety of foods, including carrion, and are known for flexible problem-solving. Their interactions and aerial movements can be as striking as their entirely black plumage.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Common Waxbill
description: The Common Waxbill is a tiny seed-eating songbird with a red facial stripe, a thick red bill in adults, and fine barring across much of its plumage. It is native to Africa and has established introduced populations in places including Hawaii. Flocks forage in grassy areas, often perching directly on stems to reach seedheads. Young birds are less brightly marked and have darker bills. Its small size and social behavior make group photographs useful for comparing individuals.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Cooper's Hawk
description: Cooper's Hawk is an agile hunter that pursues other birds through woodland and around forest edges. Its long tail and bursts of wingbeats followed by glides offer useful clues when it passes overhead. Although often elusive among trees, it also inhabits towns and suburbs, where smaller birds provide abundant prey. Females are larger than males. A quiet perched bird can be easy to overlook, making a patient scan of branches worthwhile before looking for its next sudden flight.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Dark-Eyed Junco
description: The Dark-eyed Junco is a small sparrow with several regional plumage forms, making it a useful reminder that one species can have many appearances. Most show a pale belly and white outer tail feathers that flash during flight. Juncos breed in forested habitats and often become familiar winter visitors to gardens and open woodland. They feed mainly on seeds outside the breeding season, then add insects while raising young. Much of their feeding takes place on the ground.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Double-Crested Cormorant
description: The Double-crested Cormorant is a dark waterbird often seen swimming low in the water or resting with its wings spread. It inhabits both freshwater and coastal environments across North America, diving to pursue fish beneath the surface. Adults have orange-yellow facial skin, while young birds are generally browner. The small head crests that give the species its name are most apparent during breeding. Colonies may form in trees or on relatively isolated ground near productive fishing areas.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Egyptian Goose
description: The Egyptian Goose is a sturdy waterbird with long pinkish legs, a pale head, and a distinctive dark patch around each eye. Native to Africa, it has also established populations elsewhere. It uses open landscapes near lakes, rivers, and ponds, feeding mainly on grasses, seeds, and other plant material. Much feeding takes place on land or in very shallow water. The contrast between its patterned head and broad, pale wing areas is especially noticeable when it stretches or flies.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: European Starling
description: The European Starling is a stocky songbird whose appearance changes with both season and lighting. Its dark plumage can show green and purple iridescence, while pale feather tips create a spotted pattern outside the breeding season. Native to Eurasia, it is widely established elsewhere, including North America. Starlings feed on insects, fruit, and other available foods and nest in cavities. Their social flocks, varied vocalizations, and quick movements make familiar birds worth a closer look.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Forster's Tern
description: Forster's Tern is a pale, slender seabird with narrow wings and a deeply forked tail. It searches shallow coastal and inland waters for fish, often hovering briefly before diving. Breeding birds have a dark cap, while nonbreeding birds develop a distinctive dark patch around the eye. It nests around freshwater and saltwater marshes rather than relying only on exposed ocean beaches. Photographs of feeding and interactions between birds reveal its quick movements and changing wing positions.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Fox Squirrel
description: The Fox Squirrel is a large tree squirrel with a bushy tail and variable coloring that often includes warm reddish or orange tones. Native to eastern and central parts of North America, it has also been introduced in some western urban areas. It uses trees for shelter and escape while searching both branches and the ground for food. Nuts, seeds, fruits, and other available foods make up its varied diet, and stored food helps support it through seasonal shortages.

references.title: University of Michigan: Animal Diversity Web

name: Gray Francolin
description: The Gray Francolin is a small ground-dwelling game bird with finely barred, earth-toned plumage and a contrasting throat pattern. It is native to parts of southern Asia and has been introduced to Hawaii. Dry grassland, scrub, and cultivated areas provide feeding and cover. Small groups search the ground for seeds, insects, and other foods. Their patterned feathers can blend closely with dry vegetation, while loud calls may reveal birds that would otherwise remain unnoticed.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Great Blue Heron
description: The Great Blue Heron is a large North American wading bird with a long neck, long legs, and a substantial pointed bill. It hunts fish and other small animals by waiting patiently or moving slowly through shallow water before striking. Wetlands, lake margins, and coastlines provide feeding habitat, while tall trees often support nesting colonies. In flight, it folds its neck into a characteristic curve. Its blue-gray plumage can look quite different as light and background change.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Great Egret
description: The Great Egret is a tall white heron with a long yellow bill and black legs. It hunts in shallow wetlands, often remaining motionless before making a rapid strike at a fish or other small animal. Its long neck folds into a compact curve during flight. Breeding birds develop delicate ornamental plumes, which once made egrets targets of the feather trade. Their protection became an important chapter in the development of bird conservation.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Great Frigatebird
description: The Great Frigatebird is a tropical seabird with exceptionally long wings, a deeply forked tail, and a light body built for extended flight. It searches the ocean surface for food and sometimes pursues other seabirds until they release their catch. Remote islands provide nesting places, often in trees or shrubs. Males display an inflatable red throat pouch during courtship. Its angular silhouette and effortless soaring are striking even when the bird is too distant for detailed plumage views.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Great Horned Owl
description: The Great Horned Owl is a powerful predator recognized by its prominent feather tufts, yellow eyes, and deep hooting calls. It inhabits an unusually broad range of environments, including woodland, desert, wetlands, and suburban landscapes. Mammals and birds form much of its varied diet, although it can take smaller prey as well. Its mottled plumage helps it blend into daytime roosts. Young owls look softer and less sharply patterned than adults as their flight feathers develop.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Great-tailed Grackle
description: The Great-tailed Grackle is a conspicuous, highly vocal blackbird of open country, wetlands, and developed landscapes. Males are glossy black with pale eyes and exceptionally long, tapered tails. Females are smaller and mostly brown, creating a pronounced contrast between the sexes. Groups search lawns, fields, and other open surfaces for food, then assemble in noisy roosts. The male's tail shape and iridescence are especially noticeable when viewed from different angles or in strong sunlight.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Greater Roadrunner
description: The Greater Roadrunner is a large cuckoo adapted to life on the ground in dry, open landscapes. Its long legs, raised crest, streaked plumage, and extended tail create a distinctive outline as it runs between patches of cover. It hunts insects, reptiles, and other small animals, while also taking some plant food. Although capable of flight, it often chooses to run. The long tail helps balance and steer its body during quick changes of direction.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Green Sea Turtle
description: The Green Sea Turtle is the largest sea turtle with a hard shell, paired with a comparatively small head. Its shell may be olive, brown, or gray; the common name refers to the color of its fat. Adults feed mainly on seagrasses and algae in coastal waters. Like all sea turtles, it breathes air and must surface regularly. Long migrations connect feeding areas with nesting beaches, where females return to lay eggs in sand. Juveniles can have striking patterned shells.

references.title: NOAA Fisheries: Green Turtle

name: Harbor Seal
description: The Harbor Seal is a true seal with a rounded head, short snout, and a coat patterned with spots or rings. It inhabits temperate coastal waters, feeding on fish and other marine prey. When not at sea, seals rest on beaches, rocks, reefs, or other suitable surfaces. Their small ear openings lack the external flaps seen in sea lions. A head appearing above the water may be the only visible part of an animal between dives.

references.title: NOAA Fisheries

name: Hawaiian Coot
description: The Hawaiian Coot is a dark wetland bird native to the Hawaiian Islands. Its pale bill and prominent forehead shield contrast with the body, while lobed toes help it move through water. It feeds on aquatic plants and other available foods by dabbling and diving. Ponds, marshes, and other shallow wetlands provide feeding and nesting habitat. Protecting these habitats and addressing introduced predators are important to the long-term persistence of Hawaii's native waterbirds.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Hawaiian Stilt
description: The Hawaiian Stilt, known as aeʻo, is the Hawaiian subspecies of the Black-necked Stilt. It has contrasting black-and-white plumage, a long thin bill, and exceptionally long pink legs. It searches shallow freshwater, brackish, and saline wetlands for small aquatic animals. Feeding and nesting areas may be separate, requiring regular movement between suitable sites. This album highlights the Hawaiian form, whose survival is closely connected to the protection and management of the islands' wetlands.

references.title: Hawaii Division of Forestry and Wildlife

name: Hawksbill Sea Turtle
description: The Hawksbill Sea Turtle takes its name from a narrow, pointed beak that helps it reach food in reef crevices. Its mottled shell combines amber and brown tones, typically with overlapping plates and a serrated rear edge. Many populations feed heavily on sponges, although the diet varies by region and includes other marine life. Coral reefs and sheltered coastal habitats provide feeding and resting places. Females leave the sea to nest on sandy beaches, linking their lives to both marine and coastal environments.

references.title: NOAA Fisheries: Hawksbill Turtle

name: Heermann's Gull
description: Heermann's Gull is a distinctive Pacific Coast gull with a dark gray body, a red bill, and a pale head in breeding adults. Young birds are more uniformly brown. Much of the population breeds in Mexico's Gulf of California before dispersing north along the coast. It feeds on small fish and frequently follows other seabirds, sometimes stealing their catches. Its dark plumage provides a useful contrast with the many paler gulls that share coastal resting areas.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Horned Lark
description: The Horned Lark is a small songbird of open ground, from agricultural fields and grasslands to deserts and tundra. Its brown upperparts blend closely with bare soil, while the face can show a striking pattern of pale yellow and black. Small feather tufts give the species its name. It walks across the ground searching for seeds and insects and nests in a shallow ground depression. The lack of tall vegetation is often a useful clue to its preferred habitat.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: House Sparrow
description: The House Sparrow is a small, robust songbird closely associated with people and buildings. Males have contrasting gray, brown, and black head markings, while females are more plainly patterned in brown and buff. It feeds on seeds, insects, and other available foods around gardens, farms, and towns. Native to Eurasia and parts of northern Africa, it has been introduced widely. Its busy social groups make differences in age, sex, and individual plumage easy to compare.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Iiwi (ʻIʻiwi)
description: The ʻIʻiwi is a Hawaiian honeycreeper with brilliant red plumage, dark wings, and a long, curved orange bill. It is strongly associated with native Hawaiian forest and flowering trees, drinking nectar while also taking small invertebrates. Its bill shape reflects the close connection between feeding behavior and floral resources. Today, higher-elevation forests are particularly important habitat. Habitat change and mosquito-borne disease are major conservation challenges for this distinctive bird and other native Hawaiian forest species.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Indian Peafowl
description: The Indian Peafowl is a large ground-feeding bird native to South Asia and widely kept or established elsewhere. Males, called peacocks, display an elaborate train covered in eye-like markings; females, or peahens, have more subdued plumage. The train consists of extended feathers above the true tail. Peafowl forage for seeds, fruit, insects, and small animals, then roost in trees. A displaying male turns and shakes its feathers to present the train to nearby females.

references.title: Smithsonian's National Zoo

name: Island Fox
description: The Island Fox is a small fox found only on six of California's Channel Islands, with a distinct subspecies on each island. It is related to the mainland gray fox but is much smaller. Island foxes use a range of island habitats, particularly scrub and woodland, and eat insects, fruit, and small animals according to local availability. Their restricted island distribution makes conservation especially important. Differences among the islands shape both their food choices and the challenges they face.

references.title: National Park Service

name: Island Scrub-Jay
description: The Island Scrub-Jay lives only on Santa Cruz Island off the California coast. Larger than its mainland relatives, it has rich blue upperparts, a dark face, and pale underparts. It occupies oak woodland and chaparral, where it eats acorns, insects, and other available food. Jays hide acorns for later use, linking their feeding behavior to the island's oak habitat. Pairs maintain territories throughout the year, making this bird a distinctive part of the island's wildlife.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Java Sparrow
description: The Java Sparrow is a chunky seed-eating songbird with a very large reddish bill, smooth gray plumage, and bold white cheek patches framed by a dark head. It is native to parts of Indonesia and has been introduced elsewhere, including Hawaii. Flocks feed on grass seeds and cultivated grains, often in open areas near people. Younger birds are plainer and browner. Its striking bill and face pattern stand out even among other small birds feeding on the same lawn.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Killdeer
description: The Killdeer is a plover that is often found far from the shoreline, using short grass, bare ground, gravel, and even developed areas. Two dark breast bands and a loud, repeated call help distinguish it. It searches for insects and other small animals with a characteristic sequence of quick runs and abrupt stops. Its nest is a simple scrape on open ground. Adults may use a dramatic distraction display to draw potential threats away from eggs or chicks.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Lesser Goldfinch
description: The Lesser Goldfinch is a small, social finch of open woodland, scrub, and gardens in the western Americas. Yellow underparts contrast with darker wings, while the back color of males varies across the range. These birds often gather in groups to feed on seeds, especially those of plants in the sunflower family. They may balance on bending stems as they reach seedheads. Their busy calls and varied songs can reveal a flock before its members become visible.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Little Blue Heron
description: The Little Blue Heron changes appearance dramatically as it matures. Adults have a dark blue body and a purplish head and neck, while young birds are mostly white; birds in transition can look patchy. It feeds in shallow wetlands, stalking fish and other small aquatic animals with a patient, measured approach. Like many herons, it nests in colonies, often alongside other waterbirds. Its two-toned bill and relatively compact size are useful identification clues.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Mallard
description: The Mallard is a familiar dabbling duck of ponds, lakes, marshes, and sheltered coastal wetlands across much of the Northern Hemisphere. Breeding males have glossy green heads, while females are mottled brown. Both can show a blue wing patch bordered with white. Mallards feed by reaching beneath the surface or tipping forward, taking aquatic plants and small animals. Ducklings follow their mother soon after hatching, and their changing plumage provides a clear record of early growth.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Monarch Butterfly
description: The Monarch Butterfly is recognized by orange wings crossed with dark veins and edged in black and white. Its caterpillars depend on milkweed, while adults drink nectar from many kinds of flowers. Feeding on milkweed allows monarchs to acquire chemicals that can discourage predators. Some North American populations undertake long seasonal migrations, while others remain in warmer areas. The link between milkweed for caterpillars and nectar plants for adults makes suitable habitat important throughout the life cycle.

references.title: U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service

name: Mountain Chickadee
description: The Mountain Chickadee is a small, active bird of western coniferous forests. A pale eyebrow stripe helps distinguish it from similar chickadees, alongside its dark cap, pale cheeks, and dark throat patch. It searches twigs, needles, and cones for insects and seeds, sometimes hanging upside down to reach food. Birds often join mixed flocks outside the breeding season and store food for later use. Their repeated calls can reveal a feeding flock high in the trees.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Nene (Hawaiian Goose)
description: The Nene, or Hawaiian Goose, is a native Hawaiian bird with a dark head, buff neck, and strongly textured-looking neck feathers. It spends much of its time on land, feeding on grasses and other vegetation in open habitats. Its feet are less extensively webbed than those of many other geese, reflecting its terrestrial habits. Conservation breeding, habitat management, and control of introduced threats have all contributed to efforts to protect this distinctive island goose.

references.title: Hawaii Division of Forestry and Wildlife

name: Night Heron
description: Night herons are relatively stocky wetland birds, often noticed resting quietly in vegetation or feeding around dusk. Their compact proportions distinguish them from many taller, longer-necked herons. The Black-crowned Night Heron, one useful comparison, hunts in freshwater, coastal, and brackish wetlands and nests in colonies. This album retains the broader 'Night Heron' label because the photographed bird's exact identification has not been confirmed. Head pattern, bill shape, age, and additional views can help resolve similar species.

references.title: Cornell Lab: Black-crowned Night Heron identification reference

name: Northern Cardinal
description: The Northern Cardinal is a crested songbird with a thick bill and a long tail. Adult males are bright red, while females are mostly warm brown with reddish areas on the wings, tail, and crest. It inhabits shrubby edges, gardens, and other places with dense cover, feeding largely on seeds and fruit with insects also taken. Familiar across much of eastern North America, it has also been introduced to Hawaii. Clear whistles often announce a bird before it is visible.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Northern House Wren
description: The Northern House Wren is a small brown songbird with a slender bill, short tail, and dark barring on its wings and tail. Its plain appearance contrasts with a loud, bubbling song that often reveals a bird hidden in vegetation. It searches low branches and shrubs for insects and spiders and nests in cavities, including suitable nest boxes. Gardens, parks, and open woodland provide habitat, making careful listening a useful way to locate this active and sometimes elusive bird.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Northern Mockingbird
description: The Northern Mockingbird is a slender gray songbird whose voice is often more conspicuous than its plumage. It repeats phrases and imitates the sounds of other birds, sometimes singing well into the night. Gardens, parks, and open areas with shrubs provide feeding and nesting habitat. Its diet shifts from many insects in summer toward more fruit in cooler months. White patches in the wings and tail flash during flight and territorial displays.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Northern Shoveler
description: The Northern Shoveler is a dabbling duck with an unusually broad, spoon-shaped bill. Fine structures along the bill's edges strain small aquatic animals and seeds from the water as it feeds in shallow wetlands. Breeding males show a green head, white chest, and rusty sides; females have mottled brown plumage and a prominent orange bill. Watch for birds sweeping their bills from side to side near the surface, often feeding together along the shallow margins of ponds and marshes.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Oak Titmouse
description: The Oak Titmouse is a small gray-brown songbird with a short crest and a strong association with western oak woodland. Its subdued colors can make it easy to overlook, but its active movements and frequent calls often reveal it. It searches branches and foliage for insects and also eats seeds and other plant material. Pairs defend territories throughout the year and nest in cavities. Mature trees provide both feeding opportunities and valuable nesting places.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Orange-cheeked Waxbill
description: The Orange-cheeked Waxbill is a small African songbird with conspicuous orange cheek patches and a red bill. It favors grassy habitats where seedheads provide food and dense vegetation offers cover. Birds commonly feed in groups, taking grass seeds and small insects. Their small size makes them easy to overlook until several move together through low vegetation. The contrast between the orange face and softer body colors is especially useful when comparing them with other waxbills.

references.title: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance

name: Osprey
description: The Osprey is a large fish-eating raptor associated with lakes, rivers, estuaries, and coastlines. Its pale head, dark eye stripe, and long angled wings create a distinctive appearance. It watches the water from a perch or in flight, then dives with its feet extended to seize fish. Large stick nests may be placed on trees or artificial structures. A hunting sequence shows the precision needed to turn an aerial approach into a successful underwater capture.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Pacific Golden-Plover
description: The Pacific Golden-Plover is a long-distance migrant connecting Arctic breeding grounds with islands and coastlines across the Pacific. In breeding plumage it has dark underparts bordered by pale markings and gold-speckled upperparts; winter birds are more subdued. It searches open ground for invertebrates, using quick steps followed by watchful pauses. In Hawaii it is often seen on lawns and other grassy areas. Seasonal changes in plumage can make the same species look quite different between visits.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Pacific Loon
description: The Pacific Loon is a streamlined diving bird that breeds beside northern freshwater lakes and often spends the nonbreeding season along ocean coasts. Fish make up much of its diet, captured during underwater pursuits. Breeding plumage combines a gray head with intricate dark-and-pale neck and back patterns; winter birds are more subdued. Seasonal movements can bring many loons past coastal viewpoints. Their low flights over the water connect offshore feeding areas with the changing conditions of the marine environment.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Pacific-slope (Western) Flycatcher
description: The Western Flycatcher is a small olive-and-yellow songbird of shaded western forests, often found near streams, ravines, and gaps in the canopy. It watches from a perch, then makes short flights to catch passing insects. A pale eye-ring and wing bars help describe its appearance, but its voice is especially useful for identification. Pacific-slope and Cordilleran Flycatchers were combined as Western Flycatcher in 2023; this album retains the earlier Pacific-slope wording alongside the current name.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Red Junglefowl
description: The Red Junglefowl is the wild ancestral source of the domestic chicken. Males have striking red, golden, and iridescent dark plumage, while females are more subtly patterned for concealment. In its native Asian range it inhabits forests and edges, scratching the ground for seeds, fruit, and insects. Free-ranging birds in places such as Hawaii can have domestic ancestry, so appearance alone does not establish genetic purity. This album retains the familiar Red Junglefowl label for these photographs.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Red-billed Leiothrix
description: The Red-billed Leiothrix is a small forest songbird with a red bill, olive upperparts, and warm yellow and orange coloring around the throat and breast. Native to Asia, it has established introduced populations in Hawaii and elsewhere. Dense understory provides shelter as it searches for fruit and small invertebrates. Its calls may be easier to detect than the bird itself. A brief appearance between leaves can reveal surprisingly vivid colors in an otherwise shaded forest scene.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Red-Crowned Amazon
description: The Red-crowned Amazon is a green parrot with a bright red forehead, pale bill, and a loud, social presence. Its native range centers on northeastern Mexico and nearby southern Texas, while established introduced populations occur in places including southern California. It feeds mainly on fruits and seeds, manipulating food with its bill and feet. Birds can be surprisingly difficult to see once they enter leafy trees, even when their calls make the flock's location obvious.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Red-Shouldered Hawk
description: The Red-shouldered Hawk is a woodland raptor often associated with streams, wetlands, and well-treed neighborhoods. Adults have warm barred underparts and a strongly banded tail, while pale areas near the wingtips can show when light passes through the feathers. It hunts small mammals, amphibians, reptiles, and other prey, frequently watching from a perch. Its repeated, carrying calls are useful clues to its presence, especially when the bird is partly hidden among branches.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Red-tailed Hawk
description: The Red-tailed Hawk is a broad-winged raptor commonly seen circling over open country or watching from roadside poles. It searches fields and other open areas for small mammals and a variety of additional prey. Adults usually show the reddish tail that gives the species its name, but plumage varies considerably and young birds have different tail patterns. Its combination of patient perch-hunting and effortless soaring makes it a familiar presence in many North American landscapes.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Red-Whiskered Bulbul
description: The Red-whiskered Bulbul is a lively songbird with a pointed black crest, white cheek, and small red patch beside the face. Native to parts of Asia, it has also established populations outside its original range. It uses wooded and shrubby habitats as well as gardens and other planted areas, feeding on fruit, insects, and flower buds. Its alert posture and contrasting facial markings make it distinctive, even when much of the body is concealed in vegetation.

references.title: BirdLife Australia

name: Red-winged Blackbird
description: The Red-winged Blackbird is a familiar inhabitant of marshes, wet fields, and other open habitats. Adult males are black with red-and-yellow shoulder patches that can be displayed or partly concealed. Females are brown and heavily streaked, often looking quite different from males. The birds feed on insects and seeds, with the balance changing seasonally. Males frequently sing from exposed reeds or posts, making their displays a conspicuous part of wetland breeding activity.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Reddish Egret
description: The Reddish Egret is an unusually active hunter of shallow coastal water. Instead of relying only on patient waiting, it may run, turn abruptly, and spread its wings while pursuing small fish. Dark birds have a reddish head and neck with a blue-gray body, but an all-white color form also occurs. A shaggy appearance and two-toned bill are useful features. Its rapid changes of pose make a feeding sequence particularly expressive in photographs.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Ring-billed Gull
description: The Ring-billed Gull is a medium-sized gull whose adults have a pale gray back, yellow legs, and a dark band around the bill. It is comfortable around both inland waters and coastlines, frequently using parks, fields, and developed areas as feeding grounds. Its diet is varied and opportunistic. Young birds have mottled brown plumage and different bill patterns, so age matters when identifying them. Watching a mixed flock helps reveal differences in size and proportions.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Rock Wren
description: The Rock Wren is a small songbird associated with rocky slopes, boulder fields, and other open landscapes with many crevices. Its pale, finely marked plumage blends well with stone and dry ground. It searches among rocks for insects and other small invertebrates, often making short movements between exposed perches and shelter. Nesting sites are placed in cavities or gaps among rocks. Its energetic behavior and varied voice contrast with the muted colors of its surroundings.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Rosy-faced Lovebird
description: The Rosy-faced Lovebird is a small parrot with a green body, pinkish face, pale bill, and blue rump visible especially in flight. It is native to southwestern Africa and has established introduced populations in places including Hawaii and Arizona. Social groups feed mainly on seeds, visiting grassy areas, trees, and reliable water sources. Their compact shape and short tails distinguish them from many larger parrots. Close groupings provide opportunities to observe communication, feeding, and interactions between individuals.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Ruddy Duck
description: The Ruddy Duck is a compact diving duck with a broad bill and a stiff tail that it often holds at an angle. Breeding males have chestnut bodies, white cheeks, and bright blue bills; females and winter birds are more subdued. It dives for aquatic invertebrates and other food in wetlands and sheltered waters. Courtship includes a distinctive display in which the male beats its bill against its inflated neck, producing a patch of bubbles on the surface.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Rufous-crowned Sparrow
description: The Rufous-crowned Sparrow is a ground-oriented songbird of dry, rocky hillsides with scattered shrubs and grasses. A rusty cap, pale eye-ring, and dark lines bordering the throat help distinguish its face. It often walks or hops through low vegetation, searching for seeds and small invertebrates rather than making long flights. Its subdued body colors fit closely with dry soil and rocks. A clear view of the head pattern is particularly helpful when comparing it with other brown sparrows.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Saffron Finch
description: The Saffron Finch is a small seed-eating songbird whose adult males can be intensely yellow with orange coloring on the forehead. Females and young birds are more subdued, and appearance varies among populations. Native to South America, it has been introduced elsewhere, including Hawaii. It feeds in open grassy areas, gardens, and cultivated landscapes, taking mainly seeds and some small invertebrates. Its bright plumage can make a male immediately conspicuous among birds foraging on a lawn.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Sanderling
description: The Sanderling is a small sandpiper closely associated with sandy shorelines outside the breeding season. It often runs toward retreating waves to feed, then quickly moves back as the next wave arrives. Winter birds are pale gray and white, while breeding plumage is more warmly mottled. A dark bill and dark legs remain useful features across seasons. Its rapid movements along the waterline make feeding sequences particularly lively subjects for coastal wildlife photography.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Sandhill Crane
description: The Sandhill Crane is a tall bird with long legs, a slender neck, and a distinctive red forehead in adults. Its gray plumage can take on rusty tones from staining. Cranes use wetlands and open landscapes, where their upright silhouettes are easy to recognize. Courtship brings energetic dances with leaps, wing movements, and calls. In flight, the neck extends straight ahead, offering a useful distinction from herons. Watching a pair reveals both their deliberate walking pace and expressive movements.

references.title: Alaska Department of Fish and Game: Sandhill Crane

name: Scaly-breasted Munia
description: The Scaly-breasted Munia is a small songbird with a thick seed-cracking bill. Adults have brown upperparts and pale underparts marked with dark, scale-like edges, while juveniles are plainer. Native to Asia, it has established introduced populations in several regions, including parts of the United States and Hawaii. It often feeds socially on grass seeds, clinging to stems or searching the ground. Comparing birds within a flock can reveal the transition from juvenile to adult plumage.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Snowy Egret
description: The Snowy Egret is a small white heron with a slender dark bill, black legs, and bright yellow feet. It feeds in shallow coastal and inland wetlands, sometimes using quick steps or foot movements to disturb small aquatic prey. Compared with the larger Great Egret, it often appears more animated while hunting. Fine breeding plumes once made it a target of the feather trade, and efforts to protect these birds helped advance early bird conservation.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Snowy Plover
description: The Snowy Plover is a small, pale shorebird of sandy beaches and sparsely vegetated shores. Its compact body, short dark bill, and soft upperpart colors help it blend into the ground. It searches for small invertebrates with short runs and pauses, and places its nest in a simple scrape on an open surface. Habitat disturbance can affect both feeding and nesting birds. Its subtle markings reward careful viewing, especially when it rests among sand, shells, or small stones.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Song Sparrow
description: The Song Sparrow is a widespread songbird whose appearance varies across its large North American range. Many have a streaked breast and a central dark spot, but size and overall coloring differ among populations. It uses brushy edges, marshes, gardens, and many other habitats, usually feeding near the ground on insects, seeds, and fruit. Males often leave cover to sing from exposed perches, turning an otherwise unobtrusive bird into a prominent part of the soundscape.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Spotted Dove
description: The Spotted Dove is a medium-sized dove with warm brown upperparts, a pinkish chest, and a dark neck patch dotted with pale spots. Native to Asia, it has been introduced in other regions, including Hawaii. It feeds mainly on seeds collected from the ground in gardens, fields, and open areas near trees. Its measured walking and soft calls make it a familiar presence in suitable neighborhoods. The patterned collar is an especially useful identification feature.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Spotted Towhee
description: The Spotted Towhee is a large sparrow of thickets, woodland edges, and other habitats with dense undergrowth. Males combine dark upperparts, white spotting, a pale belly, and warm reddish flanks; females show a similar pattern in softer tones. It searches leaf litter for insects, seeds, and other food, often revealing its location through rustling sounds before it is seen. Singing birds may climb into shrubs, offering a clearer view than their usual ground-level foraging.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Steller's Jay
description: Steller's Jay is a crested jay of western forests, especially landscapes with conifers. Its dark head contrasts with a blue body and wings, while harsh calls often announce its presence. It eats a varied diet that includes seeds, nuts, insects, and other animal food, and stores some food for later use. Curious and adaptable, it also visits campgrounds and forest neighborhoods. Changes in light reveal subtle patterns across the otherwise strongly contrasting plumage.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Tiger Moth Caterpillar
description: This album uses the broad Tiger Moth Caterpillar label because the exact species has not been confirmed. Many tiger moth larvae have dense bristles and are commonly called woolly bears, although appearance varies considerably among species. Caterpillars are the growing, feeding stage of the moth life cycle and later transform through a pupal stage before emerging as adults. Hair patterns, body markings, location, and food plants can help refine identification; a more specific name is left open here.

references.title: Missouri Department of Conservation

name: Tree Swallow
description: The Tree Swallow is a streamlined aerial insect hunter with glossy blue-green upperparts and white underparts in adults. It often feeds over fields, ponds, and wetlands where flying insects are abundant. Despite spending so much time in the air, it depends on cavities in trees or nest boxes for breeding. Its swift turns and glides can make flight photography challenging, while a resting bird offers a closer look at the changing iridescence of its feathers.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Tricolored Blackbird
description: The Tricolored Blackbird is strongly associated with California's wetlands and agricultural landscapes. Males have glossy black plumage and a red shoulder patch bordered below with white, a useful contrast with the yellow border of a Red-winged Blackbird. These social birds can nest in dense colonies and travel together to feed. Their reliance on suitable nesting vegetation links their conservation to both wetland habitat and the management of agricultural fields where colonies sometimes establish.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Turkey Vulture
description: The Turkey Vulture is a large scavenger often recognized in flight by wings held in a shallow V and a gently rocking glide. Adults have bare reddish heads, while young birds have darker heads. It searches broad landscapes for carrion, using a well-developed sense of smell as well as vision. Open country, woodland edges, and roadsides all provide feeding opportunities. By consuming dead animals, vultures play an important role in recycling nutrients within ecosystems.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Variegated Meadowhawk
description: The Variegated Meadowhawk is a small dragonfly associated with ponds, marshes, and other wet habitats, although adults may travel well away from water. Like other dragonflies, it has an aquatic immature stage and a flying adult stage. Adults catch small flying insects, while aquatic nymphs hunt beneath the surface. This species is capable of substantial seasonal movements. A resting individual offers a closer view of the patterned abdomen, transparent wings, and large compound eyes.

references.title: Montana Natural Heritage Program Field Guide

name: Vermilion Flycatcher
description: The Vermilion Flycatcher is a small insect-eating bird whose adult males show brilliant red plumage against dark wings and a dark face. Females are more subdued, with gray-brown upperparts and a warm wash below. It favors open habitats, often near water, and hunts by flying out from an exposed perch to catch insects. Males also perform fluttering display flights. Viewing adults, nests, and developing young together helps reveal different stages of this bird's life.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

cover.caption: Male and female · at the nest

name: Wandering Tattler
description: The Wandering Tattler is a shorebird closely associated with rocky Pacific coastlines outside the breeding season. Its gray plumage blends into wet rocks, while yellow legs and a pale eyebrow help reveal its outline. It searches the water's edge for small mollusks, crabs, and other invertebrates, often bobbing its tail as it moves. A ringing call can announce a bird before it is seen. Its migrations connect northern breeding areas with distant coastlines and islands across the Pacific.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Western Bluebird
description: The Western Bluebird is a small thrush of open woodland, meadows, and parkland with scattered trees. Adult males combine blue plumage with warm rusty areas, while females and juveniles are softer in color. It often watches from a low perch before dropping to the ground to catch insects, and also eats berries. Tree cavities and nest boxes provide nesting sites. Its upright posture and changes in plumage with age make perched photographs useful for comparing individuals.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Western Grebe
description: The Western Grebe is a long-necked diving bird with sharply contrasting dark and pale plumage, red eyes, and a pointed yellowish bill. It breeds on inland lakes with suitable marshy edges and often uses coastal waters outside the breeding season. Fish and other aquatic animals are caught underwater. Its celebrated courtship display includes paired birds rushing across the surface side by side, lifting much of their bodies above the water through rapid movements of their feet.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Western Gull
description: The Western Gull is a large gull of the Pacific Coast with a heavy bill, pink legs, and a dark gray back in adults. It nests on coastal islands and uses beaches, rocky shores, harbors, and other productive feeding places. Its varied diet includes fish and many other available foods. Young birds are mottled brown and take several years to develop adult plumage. Size, bill shape, and age-related patterns are important when comparing it with similar gulls.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Western Sandpiper
description: The Western Sandpiper is a tiny shorebird that can gather in large migratory flocks. It feeds along mudflats and shallow wetland edges, using a slender bill that is often slightly downcurved. Breeding birds show warmer markings on the head and back, while winter birds are paler. Arctic breeding grounds are connected to more southerly coastal feeding areas by long migrations. Its small size makes side-by-side comparisons with other shorebirds especially valuable for identification.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Whimbrel
description: The Whimbrel is a large, brown-patterned shorebird with a long downward-curving bill and a striped crown. It searches mud, sand, and other feeding surfaces for invertebrates, including crabs, using the bill to reach concealed prey. Migratory journeys link northern breeding areas with coastal habitats farther south. Its deliberate walking and distinctive head pattern are useful recognition clues. The broad Whimbrel album label is retained here, while current references may use the more specific name Hudsonian Whimbrel for American birds.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: White Pelican
description: White pelicans are large waterbirds with broad wings, substantial bills, and expandable throat pouches. In North America, the American White Pelican is the usual species, feeding from the water's surface rather than plunge-diving like a Brown Pelican. Groups may cooperate to concentrate fish in shallow water. Broad white wings with dark flight feathers are especially striking overhead. This album retains its original 'White Pelican' label; the American species provides the regional comparison rather than a newly confirmed identification.

references.title: Cornell Lab: American White Pelican reference

name: White-Crowned Sparrow
description: The White-crowned Sparrow is a sturdy songbird whose adult head pattern combines bold dark and pale stripes. Younger birds have softer brown-and-tan head markings, making age important when comparing photographs. It often feeds on or near the ground in brushy margins, open fields, and gardens. Many populations migrate, while some western birds remain closer to their breeding areas. Its clear, whistled song is a familiar sound, and local differences in song have attracted extensive scientific study.

name: White-faced Ibis
description: The White-faced Ibis is a long-legged wetland bird with a slender, downward-curving bill. Its dark plumage can appear plain at a distance but reveals bronze, green, and purple reflections in favorable light. Breeding adults develop a pale border around reddish facial skin and eyes. Flocks feed in shallow wetlands and wet fields, probing soft ground for invertebrates. The species' movements connect nesting wetlands with feeding areas that may be some distance away.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Wild Turkey
description: The Wild Turkey is a large ground-foraging bird of woodlands and nearby clearings. Flocks often emerge along field edges and roadsides early in the morning, walking steadily as they search for food. Courting males transform their outline by puffing up their feathers and spreading their tails, accompanied by resonant gobbling. Once greatly reduced by hunting, the species recovered through restoration efforts. A quiet woodland encounter offers a chance to appreciate its patterned feathers and the social movements of a flock.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Willet
description: The Willet is a substantial shorebird with long legs and a sturdy, fairly straight bill. Its subdued gray or mottled brown plumage can blend into beaches and mudflats, but flight reveals a bold black-and-white wing pattern. Willets feed along shorelines and in wetlands, taking a variety of small animals. Some breeding populations use inland grassland wetlands, while others nest near the coast. Their loud calls are often as useful for recognition as their appearance.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Wilson's Warbler
description: Wilson's Warbler is a small, active songbird with bright yellow underparts and olive-yellow upperparts. Males typically have a distinctive black cap, while females vary in the amount of dark coloring on the crown. It searches dense shrubs and low foliage for insects, often moving quickly between perches or hovering briefly to take prey. Willow and alder thickets, streamside vegetation, and forest openings provide useful habitat. Its restless movements can make a clear view a brief but rewarding moment.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Yellow-Crowned Night Heron
description: The Yellow-crowned Night Heron is a compact heron with a thick bill and a diet strongly focused on crustaceans, especially crabs and crayfish. Adults have gray bodies and a contrasting head pattern, while young birds are brown and spotted. It uses coastal marshes, mangroves, and other wetlands and may feed during daylight as well as at night. Patient watching followed by a quick lunge is typical hunting behavior, and the heavy bill helps handle hard-bodied prey.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Yellow-rumped Warbler
description: The Yellow-rumped Warbler is a widespread songbird with a bright yellow rump that can remain conspicuous even when the rest of its plumage is subdued. Different populations show contrasting throat and face patterns. It breeds in wooded habitats and often uses more open areas during migration and winter. Insects are important food, but an ability to eat berries helps it persist in cooler conditions. Active feeding movements can make a brief clear view particularly rewarding.

references.title: Cornell Lab of Ornithology: All About Birds

name: Zebra Dove
description: The Zebra Dove is a small, slender dove with fine dark barring across parts of its neck and body. Native to Southeast Asia, it has established introduced populations on islands including Hawaii. It feeds mainly on small seeds collected from the ground in open grassy areas, gardens, and roadsides. Its long tail and delicate proportions give it a different silhouette from larger doves. Quiet pairs or small groups can be easy to overlook until they begin moving.
